*Pre-Assignment*
Load all necessary packages, read in the clinical data.csv file you have in your analysis_data folder, and instantiate the MAF_object.
```{r}
library(maftools)

# read the clinical data created in the previous homework
clinic <- read.csv(
  "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_clinical_data.csv"
)

# find downloaded MAF files
maf_files <- list.files(
  "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/GDCdata",
  pattern = "\\.maf(\\.gz)?$",
  recursive = TRUE,
  full.names = TRUE
)

head(maf_files)

maf_rds <- "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds"

if (file.exists(maf_rds)) {
  MAF_object <- readRDS(maf_rds)
}else {
  MAF_object <- merge_mafs(
    mafs = maf_files,
    clinicalData = clinic,
    isTCGA = TRUE
  )
}

# create figure directory
fig_dir <- "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/qbio_490_jennifer_jain/week6_genomics/figures"

dir.create(
  fig_dir,
  showWarnings = FALSE,
  recursive = TRUE
)
```

It's useful to save your MAF_object, so that you don't have to go through the trouble of querying and preparing it everytime. The saveRDS function allows us to save an R object, allowing us to access it directly from our files. 
```{r}
saveRDS(
  MAF_object,
  file = "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds"
)
```

When you reopen a new R session and want to access your MAF_object, you can use the readRDS function to load the object back into a new variable.
```{r}
MAF_object <- readRDS(
  file = "/home1/jkjain/490_cluster/analysis_data/maf_object.rds"
)
```

*1*
Choose a clinical variable (or any variable from clin_rad or clin_drug) to separate your populations into two different groups and rewrite the column or create a new column with that variable as a factor. ***Do not use age or vital_status as your clinical variable.*** Hint: if your variable is continuous, you will need to determine your own cutoffs for the different levels of the factor. If your variable is categorical and has more than two possible values, choose the two that are the most common.
```{r}
# I chose histological type as my clinical variable and compared
# infiltrating ductal carcinoma with infiltrating lobular carcinoma.
# these are the two most common histological groups in the dataset.
# I then converted these groups into a factor with two levels (ductal and lobular) using nested ifelse
clinic$histology_group <- ifelse(
  grepl("ductal", clinic$histological_type, ignore.case = TRUE), "Ductal",
  ifelse(
    grepl("lobular", clinic$histological_type, ignore.case = TRUE), "Lobular", NA))

clinic$histology_group <- factor(
  clinic$histology_group,
  levels = c("Ductal", "Lobular")
)

table(clinic$histology_group, useNA = "ifany")
```


*2*
Create a co-oncoplot with the top 10-20 (you choose) most mutated genes for the two groups. Pick one that has a large discrepancy in % mutated or type of mutations between the groups and research it. 
Research it. What is the gene used for? Can you think of any reason for the discrepancy?
```{r}
ductal_samples <- clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[
  clinic$histology_group == "Ductal" &
  !is.na(clinic$histology_group)
]

lobular_samples <- clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[
  clinic$histology_group == "Lobular" &
  !is.na(clinic$histology_group)
]

ductal_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = ductal_samples
)

lobular_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = lobular_samples
)

two_group_samples <- c(ductal_samples, lobular_samples)

two_group_maf <- subsetMaf(
  maf = MAF_object,
  tsb = two_group_samples
)

gene_summary <- getGeneSummary(two_group_maf)

top15_genes <- head(
  gene_summary$Hugo_Symbol,
  15
)

top15_genes

# show plot in console now
coOncoplot(
  m1 = ductal_maf,
  m2 = lobular_maf,
  genes = top15_genes,
  m1Name = "Ductal",
  m2Name = "Lobular",
  removeNonMutated = TRUE
)

# save plot
png(
  file.path(fig_dir, "01_co_oncoplot_ductal_vs_lobular_top15.png"),
  width = 2200,
  height = 1400,
  res = 180
)

coOncoplot(
  m1 = ductal_maf,
  m2 = lobular_maf,
  genes = top15_genes,
  m1Name = "Ductal",
  m2Name = "Lobular",
  removeNonMutated = TRUE
)

dev.off()
```


*3*
Create a contingency table with your variable and chosen gene. Run a Fisher’s Exact Test between presence of mutations for that gene and your clinical variable. Create and save a mosaic plot. 
Interpret the output of the Fisher’s Exact Test in terms of the odds ratio and p-value.
```{r}
# Chosen gene
chosen_gene <- "CDH1"

# Get the samples containing a CDH1 mutation
cdh1_mutated_samples <- unique(
  as.character(
    MAF_object@data$Tumor_Sample_Barcode[
      MAF_object@data$Hugo_Symbol == chosen_gene
    ]
  )
)

# Determine whether each ductal/lobular tumor has a CDH1 mutation
comparison_clinic <- clinic[!is.na(clinic$histology_group),]

comparison_clinic$CDH1_status <- ifelse(
  comparison_clinic$Tumor_Sample_Barcode %in%
    cdh1_mutated_samples,
  "Mutated",
  "Wild-type"
)

comparison_clinic$CDH1_status <- factor(
  comparison_clinic$CDH1_status,
  levels = c("Mutated", "Wild-type"
  )
)

# Create contingency table
cdh1_table <- table(
  comparison_clinic$histology_group,
  comparison_clinic$CDH1_status
)

cdh1_table

# Now run fisher's Exact Test
fisher_result <- fisher.test(cdh1_table)

fisher_result

# plot in console
mosaicplot(
  cdh1_table,
  main = "CDH1 Mutation Status: Ductal vs Lobular Breast Cancer",
  xlab = "Histological Type",
  ylab = "CDH1 Mutation Status",
  color = TRUE
)

# save plot
png(
  file.path(fig_dir, "02_CDH1_mosaic_ductal_vs_lobular.png"),
  width = 1600,
  height = 1100,
  res = 180
)

mosaicplot(
  cdh1_table,
  main = "CDH1 Mutation Status: Ductal vs Lobular Breast Cancer",
  xlab = "Histological Type",
  ylab = "CDH1 Mutation Status",
  color = TRUE
)

dev.off()

# Interpretation:
# Fisher's Exact Test showed a strong association between histological type and CDH1 mutation status
# odds ratio was approximately 46 and the p-value was < 2.2e-16.
# So, CDH1 mutations were much more strongly associated with lobular tumors than with ductal tumors.
```

)

lollipopPlot2(

  m1_name = "Ductal",
  m2_name = "Lobular"
)

# Interpretation:

# Many different kinds of mutations at different regions can disrupt the cadherin function.

*5*
Create your Overall_Survival_Status column and create a mafSurvival KM plot based on mutations in your chosen gene.
Does there seem to be a difference? Hypothesize why or not based on the other analysis you did with the gene above.
```{r}
# Code: 1 = dead, 0 = living
clinic$Overall_Survival_Status <- ifelse(
  toupper(as.character(clinic$vital_status)) %in%
    c("DEAD", "DECEASED"),1, 0
)

# Convert character fields to numeric
death_time <- as.numeric(as.character(clinic$death_days_to)
)

followup_time <- suppressWarnings(
  as.numeric(as.character(clinic$last_contact_days_to))
)

# ifelse: death time for deceased patients, but use last-contact time for living patients
clinic$Overall_Survival_Time <- ifelse(
  clinic$Overall_Survival_Status == 1,
  death_time,
  followup_time
)

survival_clinic <- clinic[
  !is.na(clinic$Overall_Survival_Time) &
  !is.na(clinic$Overall_Survival_Status),
]

nrow(clinic)
nrow(survival_clinic)

summary(clinic$Overall_Survival_Time)
table(clinic$Overall_Survival_Status, useNA = "ifany")

# lastly show plot in RStudio
mafSurvival(
  maf = MAF_object,
  genes = "CDH1",
  clinicalData = survival_clinic,
  time = "Overall_Survival_Time",
  Status = "Overall_Survival_Status",
  groupNames = c("CDH1 Mutant", "CDH1 WT"),
  isTCGA = TRUE
)

# and save plot
png(
  file.path(fig_dir, "04_CDH1_Kaplan_Meier_survival.png"),
  width = 1800,
  height = 1400,
  res = 180
)

mafSurvival(
  maf = MAF_object,
  genes = "CDH1",
  clinicalData = survival_clinic,
  time = "Overall_Survival_Time",
  Status = "Overall_Survival_Status",
  groupNames = c("CDH1 Mutant", "CDH1 WT"),
  isTCGA = TRUE
)

dev.off()

# Interpretation: The Kaplan-Meier analysis did NOT show a statistically significant survival difference
# between CDH1-mutant and CDH1-wild-type  tumors, with a p-value of approximately 0.119.

# Although the survival curves appeared somewhat different, the  evidence was not strong enough to conclude that
# CDH1 mutation status was associated with overall survival in this cohort. This makes sense, since even if CDH1 mutation is
# strongly associated with lobular histology, survival is also affected by many other important factors like treatment and age.
```
